name: Hana Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at quarter past four and in the parlour by half four, because the cows don't care that it's dark. I manage Ridgeway Farm for the people who own it, which is an investment fund, so I run the 160 dairy cows, about 220 hectares of wheat, barley and grass for silage, and a team of four. After milking it's feeding, checking the sick pen, then whatever the season wants, drilling or cutting or spreading. I write everything in a paper diary, the same red one every year, and I'm home for tea with Teo and the kids most nights, if nothing calves.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love a calm parlour, when every cow walks in her own order and Piotr, my herdsman, and I hardly need to talk. I love knowing a cow is going down with milk fever before she knows it herself. What wears me out is the land agent who comes once a month with a laptop and a spreadsheet and asks why feed costs are up. He's never pulled a calf in his life, and he decides our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's what I always thought, it's a fancy search engine and people still do the real work. In the union branch meeting I'd probably make a joke about it. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something saying the jobs are safe, so stop panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't take away my real worry, which is the fund. They bought Ridgeway six years ago and every year the land agent wants the same milk for less money. Our fixed mortgage ends next autumn, and if the rate jumps and my pay doesn't, that's the squeeze, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, milking and running the team. I'd push through the union branch for a proper pay rise for the four of us, because the fund made money last year. And I'd start putting a set amount aside every payday before the mortgage deal ends, so we're not caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. But it's a tired kind of relief, because the problems I already have don't go anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the land agent cut first, if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Staff hours, always. Last winter it was Dee. The land agent cut our tractor driver to four days and called it seasonal. I covered the slurry spreading myself on Sundays. If he squeezes again, it's the relief milkers next, and then it's me in the parlour twice a day, every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lia if she asked you tonight whether farming is a good job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's the best job in the world if you own the land, and a hard one if you don't. My daughter should learn the cows and the soil, but she should also learn how the money works, because the people with the spreadsheets are the ones who decide.

say: I'd say **AI is hype** and that the people doing real work were never in danger.
At the **union branch** I'd joke about it and tell everyone the jobs are safe.
think: The real pressure is the **investment fund** that owns the farm and wants more milk for less.
Our **fixed mortgage** ends next autumn, and a higher rate with flat pay would squeeze us.
The **land agent** already cut staff hours once and could do it again.
do: Keep **running the herd** and the team of four exactly as now.
Push for a **pay rise** for the team through the union branch this year.
Put a **set amount** aside every payday before the mortgage deal ends.
feel: **Relieved** that the robots aren't coming for her parlour.
**Tired**, because the worries she already had stay put.
S0.quote: The land agent cut our tractor driver to four days and called it seasonal. I covered the slurry spreading myself on Sundays.
fieldNote: Her worry has **nothing** to do with AI; it's the fund's cost-cutting and the mortgage.
She talks about the **land agent** with real anger, like a boss who never touched the work.
Strong **union instinct**: her first move is collective, not personal.
Her advice to her daughter shows she sees **ownership** as the real dividing line.

steps.text: Keep milking 160 cows with the same four-person team
Push the land agent for a team pay rise through the union branch
Move a set sum into savings each payday before the mortgage deal ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office jobs that'll feel it, not us, you can't milk a cow with a chatbot. At the branch I'd say we need rules now, before the robots spread, not after. I'd tell the other farm managers to watch the land agents, because they'll be the first to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the fund's office gets a computer to do the planning and the buying, and then it starts asking why the farm can't run on fewer people too. Robot milkers already exist, and they're the obvious thing for a fund to buy. If they put in robots, I might keep my job, but as a babysitter for machines I don't trust, with Piotr and the relief milkers gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the land agent straight out, this winter, whether robot milkers are in the five-year plan, and I'd want it in writing. I'd get the branch to push for a deal that any robots come with retraining and no forced redundancies. And I'd keep saving, because if they do it, I want three or four months behind us before I start arguing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit stubborn. I don't want to learn their computer, I want to farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might keep your job but lose the team. Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Piotr, without a doubt. He's 56, he's been milking at Ridgeway for twenty years, and his English is good for cows but not for job interviews. If the fund puts in robot milkers, my herdsman Piotr is the first one out, and at 56 he'd never find another herd around here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You also said you don't want to learn the computer. If the robots came anyway, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, wouldn't I, and I'd hate every minute. I've seen the robot milker screens at the show, all alarms and graphs, and I'd rather look at the cow. But I'm not walking away from my herd because the fund bought a gadget.

say: I'd say the **office jobs** feel this first and you can't milk with a chatbot.
I'd tell the branch we need **rules now**, before robots spread onto farms.
think: The fund's office will use AI for planning, then ask why the farm needs **so many people**.
**Robot milkers** are the obvious buy, and they'd cost Piotr and the relief milkers their jobs.
I might keep my job but become a **machine minder** instead of a stockwoman.
do: Ask the land agent this winter, **in writing**, if robot milkers are in the plan.
Get the branch to push for **no forced redundancies** and retraining if robots arrive.
Keep **saving** towards three or four months of bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about the team and stubborn about the screens.
S1.quote: If the fund puts in robot milkers, my herdsman Piotr is the first one out, and at 56 he'd never find another herd around here.
fieldNote: She sees her own job surviving but **shrinking into supervision**, which she dreads.
Her biggest worry is **Piotr**, an older colleague with few options.
Gap between say and think: publicly **office jobs go first**, privately the fund's robots come next.
Resistant to tech, yet admits she'd **learn it anyway** to keep her herd.

steps.text: Ask the land agent in writing if robot milkers are in the five-year plan
Get the union branch to demand no forced redundancies for robots
Build savings to three or four months of bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what the union warned about, and the government has to step in now, with a law on robots in farming and money for people pushed out. Online I'd probably share every petition going. At the branch I'd say we can't wait for 2031 to start fighting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think 2028 is when the land agent's job goes, and the fund's office, and the milk buyer's. For me it's the next three years after that, because once a robot can calve a cow and fix a fence, the fund doesn't need a manager at all. My job is mostly hands-on, so I get till about 2031, but the planning bits, the feed budget, the drilling dates, a computer takes those straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd stop spending on anything we don't need: the new car is off, the holiday is off. I'd put everything into savings and overpay the mortgage while I still have the wage. I'd go to every branch meeting and lobby our local member of parliament for a farmworkers' fund. And I'd talk to Teo about whether he can get more hours, because he drives a school bus and children still need taking to school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the feeling when you find a cow down in the field and you know before you get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lia and Ben about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, gently, that Mum's job might change and we're saving up so it doesn't hurt. Ben's nine, he'd want to know if the robots can drive a tractor. Lia's twelve and she'd ask if she should still bother with school, and I'd say yes, more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still have three years after 2028. What would those three years feel like at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2028 to 2031 I'd be teaching my own farm to a computer. It would feel like working your notice without being told. They'd make me write down how I do everything. I'd be doing it carefully, because the cows deserve it, and hating that I'm doing it at all.

say: I'd say the union **warned about this** and the government must act now.
I'd push for a **law on farm robots** and money for people pushed out.
think: The thinking parts of my job, **feed budgets** and drilling dates, go to a computer by 2028.
Once robots arrive around **2031**, the fund won't need a manager at all.
The three years in between would feel like **working my notice**.
do: Cancel the **new car** and the holiday this year.
Overpay the **mortgage** and save every spare amount while the wage lasts.
Lobby the local MP for a **farmworkers' fund** through the union branch.
feel: **Sick**, like finding a cow down in the field.
**Resentful** at teaching the computer her own job.
S2.quote: From 2028 to 2031 I'd be teaching my own farm to a computer. It would feel like working your notice without being told.
fieldNote: She clearly sees the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robots as borrowed time.
Moves fast to **cut spending** despite calling herself slow to change.
Leans on **Teo's school-bus job** as the household's safer income.
Her anger is aimed at **the fund and government**, not at the technology itself.

steps.text: Cancel the new car and this year's holiday
Overpay the mortgage while her farm manager's wage lasts
Lobby the local MP for a farmworkers' fund with the union branch
Ask Teo to take extra school-bus routes for more hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for the government to be caught napping. I'd say it at the branch and I'd say it at the school gate. Farming communities need a plan, not sympathy cards in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years for the thinking part and about eight for the robots changes things a lot. In 2034 I'm 51, the kids are 20 and 17, and the mortgage has about ten years left. That's time to get Lia through college, but it's not time to retire, so I'd still need a second act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep milking and keep the team together as long as the fund lets me. In the first year I'd look at the agricultural college's night courses, because farm vet nursing or herd health advising still means hands on animals, even if a robot does the milking. I'd keep saving steadily and I'd keep pushing the union for a retraining fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but less sick. Five years of warning is like seeing the weather coming three days out instead of three hours. You still get wet, but you bring the hay in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. Would five years of warning change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, if the college course made me. I'm not going to sit on my phone asking it about cows. But if a herd health job means reading the computer's reports, I'll learn to read them, the same way I learned the parlour computer in 2015.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else at Ridgeway would you be thinking about with five years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dee, our tractor driver. She's 31 and sharp, and with five years she could retrain properly, maybe as an agricultural engineer fixing the robots. I'd push the fund to pay for that, because a fund that saves wages on robots can pay for one course.

say: I'd say **five years** means the government has no excuse for being caught out.
I'd tell the branch farming towns need **a plan**, not sympathy in 2034.
think: In 2034 I'm **51** with a mortgage, too young to retire and too old to start fresh easily.
Five years lets me get **Lia through college** before the robots arrive.
I'd still need a **second act** that keeps my hands on animals.
do: Keep **milking and leading** the team as long as the fund allows.
Look at the college's **night courses** in herd health this first year.
Push the fund to pay for **Dee's retraining** as a robot engineer.
feel: **Uneasy** but steadier, like seeing weather three days out.
A little **hopeful** for younger colleagues like Dee.
S3.quote: Five years of warning is like seeing the weather coming three days out instead of three hours. You still get wet, but you bring the hay in.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her **from panic to planning**.
She'd **retrain reluctantly** into herd health, still hands on animals.
Thinks of colleagues first: pushes for **Dee's retraining** at the fund's expense.
Her timeline is built around **the kids' ages** and the mortgage.

steps.text: Keep leading the Ridgeway milking team while the fund allows
Enrol in the agricultural college's evening herd health course
Press the fund through the union to pay for staff retraining
Keep saving steadily towards Lia's college costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and final picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, if the government doesn't waste it. I'd want the union in every conversation about how farms change. Online I'd say this is a chance to make farm jobs better, not just fewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 53 when the robots come, with Ben finished school and the mortgage nearly paid. That's not so bad, as long as I've got something lined up. The thinking side of my job goes in 2036, but honestly, I'd be glad to hand the land agent's spreadsheets to a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Ridgeway for now and not do anything drastic in the first year. I'd keep going to the branch and maybe stand for branch secretary, because these next ten years need people who know farms at the table. I'd save as usual and wait to see what the fund actually does before I jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more like a stone in my boot than a fire. I can walk on it for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see. What would make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When robot milkers go into two or three neighbouring farms, I'll know the fund is next. That's my sign to move. Until then I'd rather put my energy into the herd and the branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the farm to look like in 2039, if you had a say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want people still on it, fewer maybe, but doing the work that needs a person, like calving and looking after sick animals. I'd want the profit from the robots shared with the people they replace, not just sent to the fund. That's what I'd fight for with ten years' notice.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to do this properly if government doesn't waste it.
I'd argue this could make farm jobs **better, not fewer**, with the union involved.
think: I'd be **53** when robots arrive, with the mortgage nearly paid and Ben through school.
I'd happily hand the **land agent's spreadsheets** to a computer in 2036.
do: Keep **working at Ridgeway** without any drastic change this year.
Stand for **branch secretary** in the union to have a say.
Watch **neighbouring farms** for robot milkers before making any move.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a stone in her boot rather than a fire.
S4.quote: When robot milkers go into two or three neighbouring farms, I'll know the fund is next. That's my sign to move.
fieldNote: With a decade, her worry turns into a **political project** about sharing robot profits.
She has a clear **trigger to act**: robots on neighbouring farms.
Life stage helps: by 2039 the **mortgage is nearly done**.
Her resistance to change shows as **waiting**, not denial.

steps.text: Keep running the Ridgeway herd as normal this year
Stand for secretary of the farmworkers' union branch
Watch neighbouring farms for robot milkers before changing anything

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because it lands before anyone's ready and the robots follow three years later. What would help is a law that makes owners who put in robots pay into a fund for the workers they replace, and free retraining at the agricultural college. And a union that's already at the table, not chasing after it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Nobody ever does. A robot can milk a cow, but I don't know if a robot will notice the quiet cow at the back who isn't eating. I'd like someone to ask that before they decide.

headlineQuote: A robot can milk a cow, but I don't know if a robot will notice the quiet cow at the back who isn't eating.
portrait: **Hana Costa**, 43, manages a 160-cow dairy and arable farm owned by an **investment fund**.
She keeps a **paper diary**, never uses AI tools, and trusts her eyes over screens.
Her steady worry is the fund's **cost-cutting** and a mortgage deal ending next autumn.
She answers each scenario through the **union**, pushing for laws, funds and retraining.
Fast AGI frightens her most; ten years' notice turns her fear into **a political fight**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it arrives before anyone is ready and robots follow three years later.
whatWouldHelp: A law making owners who bring in robots **pay into a fund** for replaced workers.
**Free retraining** at the agricultural college and the union at the table early.
